chem-atoms-basics: Every material you can see, touch, or taste is built from atoms — roughly a hundred kinds of them, arranged in endless combinations. A single grain of sand holds more atoms than there are stars in the visible universe, and those atoms are mostly empty space. If an atom were the size of a stadium, its nucleus would be smaller than a marble at the center.
chem-nucleus-protons-neutrons: At the center of every atom sits a nucleus packed with protons and neutrons — together they make up more than 99.9% of the atom's mass while occupying almost none of its volume. Protons carry a positive charge and define which element you're holding; neutrons add mass and help glue the nucleus together against the electric repulsion of all those same-charge protons.
chem-electrons-orbitals: Orbiting the nucleus is a cloud of negatively charged electrons so light that roughly 1,800 of them weigh as much as a single proton. They arrange themselves in shells and orbitals around the atom, and chemistry is mostly the story of these electrons — how they move, share, and trade places between atoms. Everything from rust to perfume depends on that dance.
chem-atomic-number: Every element gets its identity from one number: how many protons sit in its nucleus. Change that number and you change the element itself — add a proton to iron and you get cobalt; remove one and you get manganese. That's why the periodic table is arranged by atomic number, and why chemists treat it as the element's true fingerprint.
chem-mass-number: The mass number adds protons and neutrons together, and it explains a curious thing: atoms of the same element can weigh different amounts. Those variants are called isotopes. Carbon-12 has six neutrons, carbon-13 has seven, and radioactive carbon-14 has eight — same element, different mass, and the reason carbon dating works at all.
chem-isotopes-everywhere: Isotopes aren't lab curiosities — they're part of daily life. The uranium in nuclear reactors is mostly U-238 with a sprinkle of fissionable U-235; doctors track tumors with radioactive tracers; and archaeologists date ancient remains using the slow decay of carbon-14. Even the water you drink contains a few molecules of heavier 'heavy water' made with deuterium, a hydrogen isotope with an extra neutron.
chem-valence-electrons: The electrons in an atom's outermost shell — its valence electrons — decide how it behaves chemically. Sodium has one and is eager to give it away; chlorine has seven and is desperate to gain one more; together they form table salt. The whole periodic table is organized around these outer electrons, which is why elements in the same column tend to react in similar ways.
chem-electron-shells-rule: Electrons don't orbit at random distances — they fill fixed shells, each with a capacity (2, 8, 18, 32) that determines an element's chemistry. The shells fill from the inside out, and the outermost shell is what another atom 'sees.' That's why the noble gases, with completely full outer shells, refuse to react: they have nothing to gain from meeting anyone.
chem-periodic-table-arrangement: The periodic table is a map of chemistry organized by atomic number, with rows (periods) showing shells filling up and columns (groups) gathering elements that share the same outer-electron personality. Lithium, sodium, and potassium — metals that fizz violently in water — sit in the same column because each has one outer electron. Read the structure and you can predict how an element will behave before you've touched it.
chem-mendeleev-story: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by atomic weight in 1869 — and famously left gaps where no element was known yet. He predicted the properties of those missing elements so precisely that when gallium, scandium, and germanium were discovered within fifteen years, their measured values matched his forecasts almost exactly. He reportedly saw the pattern in a dream.
chem-periodic-table-predictions: When Mendeleev left blank spaces in his 1869 table, he didn't just note that elements were missing — he predicted their atomic weights, densities, and even how they'd react. Gallium, discovered in 1875, matched his 'eka-aluminum' prediction to within a fraction of a percent. It was the moment the periodic table stopped being a list and became a law of nature.
chem-periodic-table-rows: Reading the periodic table row by row is like watching atoms get built. Each step to the right adds one proton and one electron, and the properties swing wildly: sodium, a metal that explodes in water, sits one square from magnesium, a light structural metal, and only three squares from the gas chlorine. The rows (periods) end at the aloof noble gases — full shells, no reactions wanted.
chem-groups-and-periods: The table's grid carries meaning in both directions. Columns — groups — share the same number of outer electrons, so the alkali metals in group 1 all react violently with water, and the halogens in group 17 all form salts. Rows — periods — track filling shells, so elements get progressively less metallic as you move left to right, ending each row in an inert gas.
chem-alkali-metals: Drop a lump of sodium in water and it skitters across the surface, fizzing furiously and sometimes igniting — the alkali metals in group 1 are that reactive because each has a single outer electron it's desperate to shed. Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium all do this dance, each more violently than the last. It's chemistry at its most visible: a metal giving away its one loose electron.
chem-alkaline-earth-metals: The alkaline earth metals in group 2 — beryllium, magnesium, calcium, and their kin — have two outer electrons to lose, making them reactive but calmer than their group-1 neighbors. Calcium builds your bones and shells; magnesium burns with a blinding white flame used in fireworks and flash photography. They're the 'useful metals': less explosive than sodium, more cooperative than the noble gases.
chem-transition-metals: The block of metals in the table's middle — iron, copper, gold, titanium, and dozens more — are chemistry's workhorses. Their partially filled inner shells let them take on many oxidation states, which is why iron can be Fe2+ or Fe3+, and why their compounds come in such a rainbow of colors. Most of the metals in your phone, your car, and your jewelry come from this block.
chem-noble-gases: The noble gases — helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon — have completely filled outer electron shells, so they almost never react with anything. That aloofness makes them incredibly useful: helium lifts blimps, neon glows in signs, argon shields welds from oxygen, and xenon powers car headlights. They were the last group discovered because they were so unreactive that no one noticed them for years.
chem-halogens: The halogens — fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine — sit one electron short of a full shell, making them fiercely eager to grab an electron from anyone. That hunger makes them form salts with metals (sodium + chlorine = table salt) and makes fluorine the most reactive element of all. Chlorine purifies water, iodine keeps thyroids working, and fluorine strengthens toothpaste — dangerous alone, indispensable in compounds.
chem-nonmetals-overview: Nonmetals occupy the upper right of the periodic table and play by different rules than metals: they're often gases or brittle solids, poor conductors, and hungry for electrons. Yet they run the show of life — carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen build every living thing, while chlorine, fluorine, and sulfur shape our chemistry. The split between metals and nonmetals is the table's deepest dividing line.
chem-metalloids: Along the staircase separating metals from nonmetals sits a handful of elements — silicon, germanium, arsenic, boron, and a few others — that act like both. They conduct electricity better than nonmetals but worse than metals, which makes them perfect semiconductors. Silicon's dual nature turned the entire digital age into a chemistry story: the element that's neither fish nor fowl became the heart of every computer chip.
